Data · The series

Daily net outflow, retail current accounts 1,461 days from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2025. Positive values are money leaving the bank. Five more segments have the same shape of table.

net outflow, retail current accounts
Models are fitted on the days before 03 Jul 2025 and scored on the days after.
segments6
forecast horizon14 days
history a model reads56 days
test forecasts per model1,092
Data · Eight weeks

Eight weeks of the series 7 April to 1 June 2025. Four calendar effects sit on top of the weekly cycle, and each press adds one.

Hbank holiday   Ppayday   Ddirect-debit day

Weekly cycle

Outflow is lowest on Saturday and Sunday and highest on Friday.

Payday

Salaries land on the 25th, or the last working day before it: 96 on 25 Apr. Spending rises for three days after.

Direct-debit day

Rent and bills leave on the first working day of the month: 224 on 01 May.

Bank holidays

A holiday behaves like a Sunday (78 on 18 Apr) and the held-over payments settle the next working day.

Scoring · Concept

Concept Rolling-origin evaluation: forecast 14 days, move the origin forward 14 days, repeat. The model always forecasts days it has not seen.

thirteen forecast windows
the two scores
MAE = mean |actual - forecast| in GBP million MASE = MAE / MAE of the seasonal naive forecast on the training days
MAE is in pounds, so a treasury desk can read it. It cannot be averaged across segments of different size.
MASE has no unit. Below 1, the model beats repeating last week’s value for the same weekday. Net outflow can be 0 or negative, which rules out percentage errors.
Scoring · Example

Example The seasonal naive forecast for window 1. The 14 errors below average 29.2; over all 13 windows the segment’s MAE is 27.0.

retail current accounts, 3 to 16 July 2025: red bars are the absolute errors
Sum of the 14 errors 408.7, divided by 14 = 29.2.
def seasonal_naive(o):       # o = first forecast day
    return [y[o + h - 7 * (h // 7 + 1)] for h in range(14)]
Across the six segments its MASE is 1.036, a little above 1: days 8 to 14 of each window reuse a value that is two weeks old. Every model after this slide is judged against that number.
ARIMA · Concept

Concept ARIMA forecasts a series from its own past values and its own past errors. The outflow on a given day correlates 0.51 with the day one week earlier.

autocorrelation of daily net outflow, training days
Lags 7, 14, 21 and 28 stand out: 0.51, 0.55, 0.56, 0.54.

AR: autoregression

Today is a weighted sum of the last p days. Here p = 2.

I: integration

Difference the series until it stops drifting. Here one seasonal difference: each day minus the same weekday a week earlier.

MA: moving average

Today also depends on the last q forecast errors. Here q = 1, plus one seasonal error term at lag 7.

Written ARIMA(2,0,1)(0,1,1)7: five numbers to estimate for each segment.
ARIMA · Example

Example One model per segment, fitted once in 21 seconds for all six. MASE 0.744, against 1.036 for the seasonal naive forecast.

fit = SARIMAX(y[:TEST0], order=(2, 0, 1),
              seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7)).fit()

# at each origin: new history, same weights
fit.apply(y[:o]).forecast(14)
fitted parameters, retail current accounts
ar.L1 -0.240 ar.L2 -0.002 ma.L1 0.231 ma.S.L7 -0.956 sigma2 646.032
window 2, 17 Jul to 30 Jul 2025 · Hbank holiday   Ppayday   Ddirect-debit day
MAE in this window 16.2. The forecast repeats the weekly shape and has no way to know that 25 Jul is payday.
ARIMA · Drawbacks

Drawbacks ARIMA’s error on an ordinary day is 12.3. On payday it is 75.7 and on direct-debit day 62.5.

MAE by kind of day, retail current accounts, 182 test days
  • The model sees one column: the series itself. A payday that moves between the 23rd and the 25th has no fixed lag, so no AR or MA term can catch it.
  • It is linear. An effect that grows with the size of the book is outside what it can represent.
  • Each segment gets its own model. What the corporate segment shows about bank holidays teaches the SME model nothing.
The first drawback has a classical fix: pass the calendar as regressors. That model, ARIMA + calendar, scores 0.534 and returns on the verdict slide.
Prophet · Concept

Concept Prophet writes the series as a sum of curves against the date: a trend, a weekly and a yearly cycle, and a jump for each named event.

the fitted pieces, 7 April to 1 June 2025
Add the five curves and the result is the forecast.
m = Prophet(weekly_seasonality=True,
            yearly_seasonality=True,
            holidays=bank_holidays)
for r in ['is_payday', 'sp1', 'sp2', 'sp3',
          'is_dd_day', 'post_holiday']:
    m.add_regressor(r)
m.fit(df[:TEST0])
  • Every piece can be plotted and explained to someone outside the team.
  • Events are inputs. An analyst who knows about payday adds one line.
  • The forecast for a date depends on the date alone. Yesterday’s outflow is not an input.
Prophet · Example

Example Fitted in 4 seconds for six segments. MASE 0.552; its payday error is 19.1 against ARIMA’s 75.7.

window 2, 17 Jul to 30 Jul 2025 · Hbank holiday   Ppayday   Ddirect-debit day
MAE in this window: ARIMA 16.2, Prophet 6.1.
Prophet MASE0.552
ARIMA MASE0.744
Drawback. Prophet’s error on one day correlates 0.53 with its error the day before. When outflow ran high yesterday it will run high today, and the model has no term that uses this.
Drawback. Effects add. A payday effect that is larger on a Friday, or larger in a bigger book, has to be entered by hand as another regressor.
Baselines · Verdict

Verdict Handing the calendar to ARIMA takes its MASE from 0.744 to 0.534. That is the number the deep models have to beat.

MASE over 13 windows and 6 segments, lower is better
Same test days, same 14-day horizon, weights fitted once.

What the calendar bought

ARIMA with regressors for bank holidays, payday and direct debits cuts the error by 28%. Knowing the business calendar was worth more than the choice of model.

What it cost

Somebody had to know that payday moves to the previous working day and that spending follows it for three days, and write each effect as a column.

The question for deep learning

Can a network learn those effects, and their interactions, from windows of data and a plain calendar?

LSTM · Concept

Concept Forecasting becomes supervised learning: slide a 70-day window along each series, give the network the first 56 days and ask for the last 14.

one square is one day

One model, six segments

Windows from every segment go into the same network, with the segment as an input. Each series is scaled by its own mean and standard deviation first.

The calendar is an input

Weekday, bank holiday, payday, days since payday and direct-debit day, for the 56 past days and the 14 future ones. The future calendar is known today.

No effect is written by hand

The network is not told that payday lowers outflow or that spending follows it. It has to find that in the windows.

LSTM · Mechanism

Mechanism One LSTM cell processes one day. Three gates, each a vector of numbers between 0 and 1, decide what the memory keeps, takes in and shows.

one cell, one time step
the six lines
f = σ(W_f · [h(t-1), x(t)]) forget i = σ(W_i · [h(t-1), x(t)]) input g = tanh(W_g · [h(t-1), x(t)]) candidate o = σ(W_o · [h(t-1), x(t)]) output c(t) = f × c(t-1) + i × g h(t) = o × tanh(c(t))
The cell state changes by a multiplication and an addition, so a value written on day 1 can survive to day 56. A plain recurrent network rewrites its whole state every step and loses it.
With a hidden size of 64, each gate is 64 numbers. The whole forecasting network on the next slide has 44,889 weights.
LSTM · Mechanism

Mechanism continued 1 The forecaster is two LSTMs. The encoder reads 56 days and hands its final state to the decoder, which steps through the next 14 days of calendar.

encoder in blue, decoder in red
class Seq2Seq(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_known=17, hidden=64, n_seg=6):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(n_seg, 4)
        self.enc = nn.LSTM(1 + n_known + 4, hidden, batch_first=True)
        self.dec = nn.LSTM(n_known + 4, hidden, batch_first=True)
        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden, 1)

    def forward(self, xe, xd, sid):
        e = self.emb(sid)                                  # segment -> 4 numbers
        _, state = self.enc(cat(xe, e))                    # read the past
        d, _ = self.dec(cat(xd, e), state)                 # step through the future
        return self.out(d).squeeze(-1)                     # 14 forecasts
17 calendar inputs: 7 for the weekday, then bank holiday, payday, three flags for the days after payday, direct-debit day, day after a holiday, and three for the time of year.
Loss: mean absolute error on the scaled outflow. Training stops when the validation loss has not improved for 8 epochs.

LSTM · Drawbacks

Drawbacks Five runs that differ only in the random seed score between 0.541 and 0.582. ARIMA with the calendar scores 0.534 every time.

MASE of the same network trained five times
MAE by kind of day: ARIMA + calendar in slate, LSTM in purple

It matched the baseline

The LSTM learned the calendar effects from windows: its payday error is 19.8, ARIMA + calendar 19.5. On six series with additive effects that gave no clear gain.

One number per day

The output is a point forecast. A treasury desk sizing a buffer needs to know how wrong the forecast can be, and this network does not say.

No account of itself

Prophet shows its curves and ARIMA its five weights. The LSTM has 44,889 weights and no part of it reads as the payday effect.

Deep forecasters pull ahead with hundreds of related series, inputs that interact, and long histories. With six series and effects that add up, a classical model given the right columns is hard to beat.
TFT · Concept

Concept The Temporal Fusion Transformer keeps the LSTM and adds three parts around it: typed inputs with learned weights, attention over the past, and quantile outputs.

Lim et al., 2021, simplified

Variable selection

A small network gives each input a weight at every step. The weights can be read afterwards.

LSTM

The same encoder and decoder as the last section, for local patterns such as the weekly cycle.

Attention

Each forecast day looks back over all 56 encoder days and weights them. The weights show which past days it used.

Quantiles

Three outputs per day. P10 to P90 is a range the outflow should fall inside on 8 days in 10.

TFT · Mechanism

Mechanism A quantile forecast is trained with the pinball loss, which charges q per unit for forecasting too low and 1 - q for too high. Below: the outflow on 23 ordinary Wednesdays of the test period.

dots: the Wednesdays · curve: the loss of forecasting each value for all of them
browser JS
pinball loss for one day
loss = q × (y - ŷ) if y ≥ ŷ (1 - q) × (ŷ - y) otherwise
At q = 0.5 the two costs are equal and the best forecast is the median. At q = 0.9 a forecast that is too low costs nine times as much, so the minimum moves up until 90% of the values lie below it.
TFT · Example

Example 84,383 weights, 14 epochs, 260 seconds on a CPU. The median forecast scores MASE 0.533, and the P10 to P90 band holds the actual outflow on 71.8% of test days.

training = TimeSeriesDataSet(
    long[long.time_idx < VAL0],
    time_idx='time_idx', target='net_outflow',
    group_ids=['segment'],
    max_encoder_length=56, max_prediction_length=14,
    static_categoricals=['segment'],
    time_varying_known_categoricals=['dow', 'since_payday'],
    time_varying_known_reals=[...calendar flags...],
    time_varying_unknown_reals=['net_outflow'],
    target_normalizer=GroupNormalizer(groups=['segment']))

tft = TemporalFusionTransformer.from_dataset(
    training, hidden_size=32, attention_head_size=4,
    loss=QuantileLoss([0.1, 0.5, 0.9]))
A band built to hold 80% of days held 71.8%. The outflow was above P90 on 12.3% of days and below P10 on 15.9%. A quantile forecast has to be backtested before a buffer is sized from it.
window 2, median and P10 to P90 band · Hbank holiday   Ppayday   Ddirect-debit day
MAE of the median in this window 7.7.

Example continued 1 What the model reports about itself. For the future days the largest selection weight is on dow (22.2%); for the past, 56% is on the outflow itself.

The three most attended days are 55, 48, 34 days before the origin.
These weights describe where the network looked. They are a starting point for a conversation with the treasury desk, not a causal statement about what drives outflow.

The step that mattered was from 0.744 to about 0.53, and it came from the calendar. Which model consumed the calendar changed the score by 0.019.
What the deep models add here is in the output: one model for all segments, a quantile band, and weights that can be inspected. Start with the baseline, and move up when one of those is needed.
Applications

Forecasting problems in a bank The models are the same. The target, the horizon and the inputs known in advance change with the problem.

Cash-flow forecasting

Target: daily net outflow by segment or legal entity.
Horizon: 1 to 30 days.
Known in advance: payday, direct-debit dates, bank holidays, tax deadlines, scheduled maturities.
Feeds: intraday funding and the treasury plan.

Demand forecasting

Target: cash drawn per ATM, calls per hour, logins per minute, mortgage applications per week.
Horizon: hours to weeks.
Known in advance: calendar, campaigns, rate announcements.
Feeds: cash replenishment, staffing, capacity.

Market forecasting

Target: volatility, volumes, spreads. Price direction has almost no forecastable signal at a daily horizon.
Horizon: minutes to days.
Known in advance: central bank dates, data releases, expiries.
Feeds: risk limits, margin, hedging.

Many related series favour one shared model. With 5,000 ATMs or 400 branches, one model trained across all of them replaces 5,000 separate fits. The ATM slides measure this on 200 ATMs.
The cost of an error is lopsided. An empty ATM costs more than a full one, and a funding shortfall more than idle cash. That asymmetry is the q in the pinball loss, which is why these problems are forecast as quantiles.
In every case the test is the one used today: hold back the most recent period, forecast it from an earlier origin, and compare against the seasonal naive forecast.
Applications · Liquidity risk

Concept A treasury desk holds cash today against tomorrow’s outflow. The forecast it acts on is a high quantile: an amount that should be enough on 9 days in 10.

retail current accounts, forecast made on 22 Oct for 23 Oct to 05 Nov · Hbank holiday   Ppayday   Ddirect-debit day
days above the median8 of 14
mean outflow per day132
days short of the P906 of 14
short, total66.6
cash held, not used175.0
per day12.5
The decision is the green line. A point forecast answers what will happen. The desk asks how much to hold, and that is a quantile of the same forecast.
Two costs pull against each other. Cash held and not used earns less than it would elsewhere. A short day is covered by borrowing at a worse rate. A higher line trades one for the other.
Applications · Liquidity risk

Example Sized from the TFT’s P90, the two-week buffer was exceeded in 0 of 13 windows; sized from the median, in 8.

retail current accounts, cumulative outflow per window
windows above the P90 buffer0 of 13
windows above the median buffer8 of 13
A buffer sized from the median forecast is too small about half the time by construction. The desk holds a high quantile, and the question for the next slide is whether the P90 behaves like one.
Adding 14 daily P90s gives more than the P90 of the 14-day total, because the days do not all run high together. To size a two-week buffer exactly, train the model on the cumulative outflow or sample whole paths.
Applications · Liquidity risk

Test Backtest the quantile. A P90 should be exceeded on 10% of days; for retail current accounts it was exceeded on 33 of 182, which is 18.1%.

retail current accounts · red above P90 · blue below P10 · grey inside the band
33 red and 27 blue of 182. The band was meant to hold 80% of days and held 67%, so it is too narrow on both sides.
days above the P90, all six segments, with a binomial test against 10%
4 of 6 segments fail the test, three with a P90 that is too low and SME with one that is too high. The test counts days as independent. Red days here arrive together, 0 to 6 in a window, so the p-values overstate the evidence.
A desk runs this count every week on the newest days. When the rate drifts from 10% it widens the margin from recent errors, which is the next slide, or retrains.
Applications · Liquidity risk

Cost Hold the forecast plus a fixed margin. To be short on 9 of 182 days the margin is 58.0 with the seasonal naive forecast, 45.9 with ARIMA and 25.0 with the TFT.

browser JS
left: actual minus forecast, 182 test days, retail current accounts · red: short that day  |  right: cost per day against the margin
Accuracy is paid back as cash. For the same 9 short days the TFT desk holds 37 million a day less idle cash than the seasonal naive desk, on one segment with a mean outflow of 125 million a day.
The multiple picks the quantile. If a pound short costs 9 times a pound idle, the cheapest margin is the 90th percentile of the errors: 9 / (9 + 1). That multiple is the q in the pinball loss.
Applications · The whole bank

Example The desk funds the bank, which is the six segments added. The TFT’s six errors add to 58.1 million a day, and its error on the total is 28.9.

TFT, 182 test days · mean net outflow of the bank 457 million a day
days above the six P90s added3 of 182
that is1.6%
Six P90s added are far above a P90. The segments do not all run high on the same day, so the sum was exceeded on 1.6% of days and the bank holds more than the 10% target asks for.
32 million a day is released by sizing the margin on the total: 44.8 against 76.4. Forecast the quantity the decision is made on, or sample the six segments together.
The same arithmetic applied across days on the earlier slide: 14 daily P90s added were never exceeded in 13 windows.
Applications · Horizon

Example The second week against the first. The TFT scores 0.534 on days 1 to 7 and 0.532 on days 8 to 14; ARIMA goes from 0.713 to 0.775.

13 windows, 6 segments; each week holds every weekday once
3 models lose nothing in week 2: Prophet, LSTM, TFT. Paydays, direct-debit days and bank holidays for day 14 are known on day 0, and most of this series is calendar.
Both ARIMA models lose about 0.06. Part of their forecast comes from the last few days’ errors, and that information is used up within a week.
Which horizon the desk needs depends on the decision: tomorrow for intraday funding, two weeks for the funding plan, 30 days for a liquidity ratio. Only 14 days was tested here. A 30-day claim needs its own backtest.
Applications · ATM cash

Concept A second problem with the same shape. 200 ATMs, cash withdrawn per day for 731 days, and a van that loads each one for the days until its next visit.

GBP thousand withdrawn per day, the 6 weeks before the test · pale bars are weekends · Ppayday Hbank holiday
ATMs200
opened 90 days before the test20
mean withdrawn per day14.4
test days91
The decision is the load. Too little and the ATM is empty before the van returns. Too much and cash sits in a box earning nothing. A third cost is new here: each visit is paid for.
The week differs by site. A transport hub is busy Monday to Friday, a high street on Friday and Saturday, and a residential ATM after payday.
20 ATMs are new. Each has 70 days to train on, so a model fitted to one of them alone learns its payday and its week from those 70 days.
Applications · ATM cash

Example One model trained on all 200 ATMs scores MASE 0.656. 200 models, one per ATM, score 0.732, and the seasonal naive forecast 0.947.

gradient-boosted trees, median forecast, 7 days ahead, 13 weekly origins
Same model class, same inputs. Weekday, payday, bank holiday, December, days ahead and the ATM’s mean over the last 28 days. The shared model also reads the kind of site and the ATM id.
Pooling helps the established ATMs too: 0.644 against 0.720. A payday at one residential ATM teaches the model about the other 77.
New ATMs: 0.758 against 0.842. The shared model forecasts an ATM with 70 days of history almost as well as the per-ATM models forecast one with two years (0.720).
One model to maintain. The shared fit took 29 seconds for five quantiles; the 200 separate fits took 105 seconds for the median alone.
Applications · ATM cash

Test Backtest the P95 one ATM at a time. Over all 18,200 ATM-days it was exceeded on 4.2%, close to the 5% it promises. 10 ATMs were above it on 10 days or more.

one square is one ATM · red: 10 or more days above
forecastshould be exceededwas exceeded
P5050%41.5%
P8020%15.6%
P9010%7.8%
P955%4.2%
P991%1.0%
The average passes and 10 ATMs fail. With a true 5%, ten or more days above in 91 has a probability under 2% for one ATM. These 10 run out more than their share however the fleet average looks.
The backtest is run at the level the cash is held, which here is the single ATM. The red ATMs get a higher quantile or a look at what changed at the site.
Applications · ATM cash

Cost Two choices: the quantile to load to and the days between visits. The P95 every 3 days leaves 0.32% of ATM-days empty and 36.0 thousand in each ATM at day end.

browser JS
left: cash in one residential ATM over the 91 test days under the chosen policy  |  right: all 20 policies for the 200 ATMs, the chosen one circled
Fewer visits cost cash. At the P95, a daily visit leaves 7.5 thousand in each ATM at day end and a weekly visit 93.0. The van is saved 6 trips a week per ATM.
A longer cycle is safer than its quantile says. Loading to the P95 daily leaves 4.1% of ATM-days empty, and weekly 0.04%, because 7 daily P95s added are far above the P95 of a week.
Applications · Call volumes

Concept A third problem. One contact centre, calls counted every half hour, and a roster written a week ahead that needs a number of agents for each half hour.

simulated contact centre · mean handling time 5 minutes
half hours in the test2,184
mean calls per half hour102
Two cycles at once. Monday is the busy day and each weekday has a morning and an afternoon peak. The forecast is needed per half hour because agents are rostered per half hour.
The cost of being short is steep. With 100 calls in a half hour, 21 agents answer 83% within 20 seconds. Two fewer answer 59%, and 17 answer 11%.
The formula is Erlang C. It takes calls per half hour and handling time and returns the agents needed. The forecast is its input, so a forecast error becomes a queue.
Applications · Call volumes

Test The P90 was exceeded in 290 of 2,184 half hours, 13.3%. Half of those misses fall on 10 of the 91 days.

red: calls above the P90 forecast for that half hour
The red comes in columns. 36 days have no red half hour and 13 days have 8 or more.
MASE, seasonal naive0.872
MASE, model0.578
A busy day is busy all day. The day’s total ran between 0.84 and 1.21 times its forecast on 9 days in 10, and every half hour of that day moved with it.
Half hours are not independent trials. A count of red cells understates how bad a red day is for the people on the phones: the queue from 10:00 is still there at 10:30.
A first version failed this test. Trees fed raw call counts were exceeded on 24.3% of half hours. The level in the test reached 107 calls and training had seen 101, and a tree cannot forecast above what it has seen. The model here forecasts calls divided by the recent level.
Applications · Call volumes

Example The morning is a measurement of the day. Scaling the afternoon forecast at 12:00 by the morning’s ratio takes the afternoon error from 10.6 to 7.9 calls per half hour.

Sat 2025-12-13, the test day with the largest morning ratio
morning, actual / forecast1.38
days the update helped64 of 91
afternoon MAE, weekly forecast10.6
after the 12:00 update7.9
The update is one multiplication: calls received by 12:00 divided by calls forecast by 12:00, applied to every half hour left.
It made 27 days worse. On an ordinary day the morning ratio carries more noise than signal, so a production version shrinks it toward 1.
The roster is fixed, so the update buys the afternoon’s levers: moved breaks, overtime, call-backs offered.
Applications · Call volumes

Cost Roster to the median forecast and 61% of half hours meet the target. Roster to the P90 and 90% do, for 36 more agent-hours a day.

browser JS
left: one test day, calls received against the forecast the roster was written for  |  right: the four rosters over all 91 days
The price of not knowing. With the calls known in advance the target needs 254 agent-hours a day. The P90 roster uses 290 and still misses in 10% of half hours.
The median is the wrong forecast to roster to. Being 10% short costs far more service than being 10% over costs in wages, so the roster follows a high quantile. On 60 of 91 days the median roster had 6 or more half hours below target.
Applications · Drawbacks

Drawbacks Where a forecast misleads the people who act on it, with the number measured in this session.

What goes wrongMeasured hereWhat the desk does
The band is the wrong widthP90 exceeded on 18.1% of days for retail current and 3.8% for SME, against 10%Backtest each segment on the newest days.
Quantiles do not addSix P90s added: exceeded on 1.6% of days. 14 daily P90s added: exceeded in 0 of 13 windowsForecast the total and the period the buffer is held against.

Trees do not extrapolateCall model on raw counts: P90 exceeded in 24.3% of half hours. On calls divided by the recent level: 13.3%Scale the target by a recent level when the series trends.
The history holds ordinary days1,461 days, none of them a run on depositsThe forecast sizes the day-to-day buffer. A stress buffer comes from regulatory scenarios.
The desk is scored on the breach rate and the cash held. MASE ranks the models; the backtest and the margin decide how much money sits idle.
Four steps served all three problems: forecast a quantile, backtest it, price the two errors, forecast at the level of the decision.
GAN · Concept

Concept A generator turns random numbers into a table row. A critic scores rows, and each network is trained against the other.

conditional GAN on one transaction row
The generator does not read real rows. What reaches it is the gradient of the critic’s score.
Use case at a bank: a vendor, a test environment or another team needs transaction data, and the real table cannot leave. A generator trained on the real table writes rows with the same statistics and no real customer in them. The three tests later in this section measure how far that holds.

The held-out rows are real rows the GAN does not see. They give every test a reference: the score two samples of real data produce against each other.
GAN · Mechanism

Mechanism The training loop, abridged from the notebook. 150 epochs of 103 batches took 318 seconds on a laptop CPU.

for step in range(STEPS):
    x, c = real_batch()                        # 512 rows, 20% of them fraud
    fake = G(noise(), c).detach()
    gap = C(x, c).mean() - C(fake, c).mean()   # critic's distance estimate
    lossC = -gap + 10 * gradient_penalty(C, x, fake, c)
    optC.zero_grad(); lossC.backward(); optC.step()

    if step % 5 == 0:                          # 1 generator step per 5 critic steps
        lossG = -C(G(noise(), c), c).mean()
        optG.zero_grad(); lossG.backward(); optG.step()
  1. Wasserstein loss. The critic outputs an unbounded score, and the gap between its mean score on real and generated rows estimates the distance between the two tables.
  2. Gradient penalty. It keeps the critic’s slope near 1, which is what makes that gap a distance.
  3. Oversampled fraud. Fraud is 0.90% of the table, about 5 rows in a batch of 512. Each batch is drawn with 20% fraud so the generator learns that class.
the gap the critic measures
The gap falls from 4.1 to 0.82 as generated rows become harder to separate.
Generator 87,057 weights, critic 70,913. Numeric columns pass through a quantile transform and the two categorical columns are one-hot.

GAN · Test 2: utility

Test continued 2 Train the fraud classifier on the synthetic table and test it on the real last 60 days. ROC-AUC drops from 0.904 to 0.884 and PR-AUC from 0.346 to 0.235.

m_real  = fraud_model(fit)
m_synth = fraud_model(synth)
evaluate(m_real), evaluate(m_synth)
ROC-AUC keeps 98% of its value: the synthetic table ranks transactions almost as well. PR-AUC keeps 68%: the precise shape of the 477 fraud rows, which decides the top of the ranking, is the part the generator reproduces least well.
This test is the one to quote to a team that will build models on the synthetic table. It answers their question directly.
GAN · Test 3: privacy

Test continued 3 Distance to the closest record. 5.6% of GAN rows sit closer to a training row than the 5th percentile of held-out real rows; for a noisy copy of the training table it is 99.7%.

13,287 rows of each kind, distance in the encoded space
Median distance: held-out 0.489, GAN 0.535, noisy copy 0.115.
  1. For each synthetic row, find the nearest training row and record the distance.
  2. Do the same for real rows the generator did not see. Those distances are what an honest table produces.
  3. Compare. A generator that memorised its training rows produces distances near 0.
Second check: is a synthetic row nearer to a training row or to a held-out row? GAN rows choose the training row 50.2% of the time, the noisy copy 99.9%. 50% means the generator shows no preference for rows it was trained on.
The test clears the GAN table and condemns the copy. 0 of 53,148 synthetic rows equal a training row.
GAN · Drawbacks

Drawbacks What the three tests found, and what they cannot show.

Rules are learned as tendencies

2.96% of rows break a rule that every real row obeys. Validate synthetic rows with the checks the production table already passes.

The rare class is the weakest

PR-AUC on fraud falls to 68% of the real-data value. 477 fraud rows are a small sample to learn a distribution from, and they are the rows a fraud team cares about.

Distance is evidence, not proof

The closest-record test shows no copying on this run. It gives no bound on what an attacker who holds the generator can infer about one customer.

A formal guarantee needs differential privacy: train with DP-SGD, which clips each row’s gradient and adds noise, and report the privacy budget ε. Fidelity and utility fall as ε shrinks, so the three tests are run again at the chosen ε.
Before a synthetic table leaves the bank, three numbers go with it: the fidelity gaps, the train-on-synthetic score, and the closest-record result. Rare categories and outliers are checked by hand, because one extreme row can identify one customer.
Other generators for tables: CTGAN and TVAE (the SDV library) handle mixed column types out of the box, and diffusion models now match or beat GANs on tabular fidelity. The three tests apply to all of them unchanged.
Fraud pipeline · Concept

Concept A fraud model is one box in a loop. The threshold, the analysts and the delay before a label arrives are design decisions of the same weight.

from a transaction to a confirmed label
Labels arrive late and only for transactions somebody reviewed or disputed, so the training table is always behind the fraud.

Scoring

The score is needed before the payment is authorised. Features that need a lookup, such as transactions in the last 24 hours, are kept current by a stream job.

Threshold

A team of analysts reviews a fixed number of alerts a day. The threshold is whatever score fills that number.

Feedback

Fraudsters change behaviour once a pattern is blocked. The model is retrained on a schedule and its score distribution is monitored between retrains.

The isolation forest flags rows that are unusual. Unusual and fraudulent overlap only in part: a large travel purchase is rare and genuine. It is the detector to run while labels do not exist yet, and a feature for the supervised model afterwards.
Fraud pipeline · The alert budget

The alert budget The threshold follows from how many alerts the analysts can review. Move the budget and read what it buys on the 281 fraud rows worth £40,859.

browser JS
60 test days
Each extra alert a day costs analyst time and finds less fraud than the one before it. The budget is set where the value of the next fraud caught equals the cost of the reviews needed to find it.
A blocked genuine payment has a cost as well: a customer at a till with a declined card. That cost sits in the precision bar.
Fraud pipeline · GAN fraud rows as training data

Example continued 1 Adding generated fraud rows to the training set moved PR-AUC from 0.359 to at most 0.367. Repeating real fraud rows reached 0.377.

mean of 5 runs, bars show one standard deviation
class_weight='balanced' on the same model scores 0.327.
fake_fraud = sample(G, k, cond=torch.ones(k, 1))
model = fraud_model(pd.concat([train, fake_fraud]))
The generator learned fraud from 477 rows. Its samples carry no information beyond those rows, and they blur the boundary the classifier is trying to find. On this table the cheap method, repeating real fraud rows, did at least as well.
Where generated fraud does earn its place: testing. A rule engine, an alert queue or a new model can be load-tested on a stream with 10% fraud without waiting months for real cases.
Fraud pipeline · Checks to run before deployment

Checks to run before deployment Each check is one line on the tables in the notebook, with the output it gave.

1. Split by time.

train, test = tx[tx.day < 120], tx[tx.day >= 120]
66,435 rows before day 120, 33,565 after

2. Score on the fraud rows.

average_precision_score(test.is_fraud, score)
0.361 (accuracy of flagging nothing: 99.16%)

3. Set the threshold from the alert budget.

top = np.argsort(-score)[:10 * 60]     # 10 alerts a day
138 of 281 fraud rows caught, precision 23%

4. Watch the score distribution after release.

psi(score[first_30_days], score[last_30_days])
0.0012 (0.2 is the conventional alarm level)
A random split lets the model train on transactions from after the ones it is tested on. In production it scores the future, so the test has to be the future as well.
The simulated table has no drift, which is why the PSI is near 0. Real fraud moves, and the PSI of the score is the first place that shows.

Forecasting. Score every model against the seasonal naive forecast on held-back days. Put the business calendar in before changing the model. Move to an LSTM or TFT for many related series, interacting inputs, or a quantile, and backtest the quantile.
Generative models. A synthetic table is released with three test results: fidelity, utility, privacy. In a fraud pipeline the threshold comes from the alert budget, the split is by time, and generated fraud is for testing systems more than for training models.
